entities.name: Johann Amadeus Francis de Paula, Baron of Thugut
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johann Amadeus Francis de Paula, Baron of Thugut, served as Austria's influential foreign minister from 1793 to 1801, spearheading a staunchly anti-French policy during the tumultuous early years of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Born in 1736, Thugut's career spanned a period of profound upheaval, wherein he guided Habsburg diplomacy through the collapse of the Old Regime and the rise of a new European order dominated by France. His tenure was defined by a relentless commitment to preserving Austrian power and tradition against the revolutionary tide, positioning him as a central, if often controversial, figure in the First and Second Coalitions against France.

Thugut's diplomatic ascent began with missions to the Ottoman Empire and the Kingdom of Naples, where he gained invaluable experience in complex international relations. Appointed foreign minister by Emperor Francis II in 1793, he immediately confronted the existential threat posed by revolutionary France. He orchestrated Austria's participation in the First Coalition, suffering significant setbacks culminating in the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797, which ceded the Austrian Netherlands and Lombardy to France. Undeterred, Thugut was a principal architect of the Second Coalition in 1798, aiming to reverse French gains and restore the Bourbon monarchy. Despite initial successes, this coalition also crumbled under French military might, notably after Napoleon's victory at Marengo in 1800, leading to the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801 and Thugut's eventual resignation.
